subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Total internal reflection is used in optical fibres. What must be true for it to occur?
options: The fibre must be perfectly straight
Light must travel from a more dense to a less dense medium, above the critical angle
Light must travel from a less dense to a more dense medium
questions.explain: For total internal reflection the light must be going from a more optically dense medium (the glass core) into a less dense one, striking the boundary above the critical angle, so it reflects rather than refracts out.

questions.q: Total internal reflection can occur when light travels from glass into air and the angle of incidence is:
questions.explain: Total internal reflection happens when light moving from a denser to a less dense medium hits the boundary at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle, so all the light is reflected back inside.

questions.q: What is the approximate range of frequencies that a healthy young human ear can hear?
questions.explain: The normal human hearing range is about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz (20 kHz). Sound above this range is called ultrasound.

questions.q: For total internal reflection to take place, light must be travelling in the denser medium and strike the boundary at an angle of incidence that is:
questions.explain: Total internal reflection occurs when light moves from a denser to a less dense medium and the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle, so all the light reflects back inside.

questions.q: A red book looks red in white light because it:
options: Reflects red light and absorbs the other colours
Absorbs red light and reflects all other colours
questions.explain: An opaque coloured object reflects the colours we see and absorbs the rest. A red book reflects red light and absorbs the other colours of white light.

questions.q: A blue object is viewed under pure red light. It will appear:
questions.explain: A blue object reflects only blue light and absorbs others. Under red light there is no blue light to reflect, so it absorbs the red and appears black.

questions.q: Total internal reflection is used to carry light along optical fibres. Which other application relies on it?
options: An endoscope used to see inside the body
questions.explain: Endoscopes and optical fibres use total internal reflection to guide light (and images) along curved fibres without it escaping the sides.

questions.q: When a wave is reflected from a flat surface, how does the angle of reflection compare with the angle of incidence (both measured from the normal)?
options: The wave is absorbed, not reflected
The angle of reflection is smaller
The angle of reflection is larger
questions.explain: For reflection, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal to the surface.

questions.q: In a moving-coil microphone, what causes the electrical signal to be generated?
options: Sound waves move a coil near a magnet, inducing a changing p.d.
questions.explain: In a microphone, sound waves make a diaphragm and attached coil vibrate near a magnet. The changing magnetic field through the moving coil induces an alternating p.d. — the generator effect — which matches the sound.

questions.q: A sound wave with a frequency above 20 000 Hz is called:
questions.explain: Sound above the upper limit of human hearing (about 20 kHz) is called ultrasound. Sound below 20 Hz is infrasound.

questions.q: Sound waves cause our eardrums to vibrate so we hear. Why can't sound travel through a vacuum?
options: There are no particles in a vacuum to vibrate and carry the wave
questions.explain: Sound is a longitudinal wave that needs particles in a medium to oscillate and pass on the vibration. A vacuum has no particles, so sound cannot travel through it.

questions.q: A surface that scatters light in many directions, rather than forming a clear image, produces:
questions.explain: A rough surface causes diffuse reflection: the normals point in many directions so reflected rays scatter. A smooth surface gives specular reflection and a clear image.

questions.q: A red jumper looks red in white light because it:
options: Reflects red light and absorbs the other colours
Lets all colours pass through it
Adds red light to the white light
questions.explain: An opaque coloured object reflects the colours of light it appears and absorbs the rest. A red jumper reflects red wavelengths and absorbs the other colours of the spectrum.

questions.q: A converging (convex) lens is used as a magnifying glass. What type of image does it form when the object is closer than the focal length?
options: Real, upright and the same size
questions.explain: When the object is within the focal length of a converging lens, the lens acts as a magnifying glass, producing a virtual, upright, magnified image on the same side as the object.

questions.q: Which colour of visible light has the longest wavelength?
questions.explain: Within the visible spectrum, red light has the longest wavelength and lowest frequency, while violet has the shortest wavelength and highest frequency.

questions.q: A converging (convex) lens is used as a magnifying glass. Which type of image does it form when an object is very close to the lens?
options: A real image the same size
questions.explain: When an object is closer than the focal length of a convex lens, the lens produces a virtual, upright and magnified image — this is how a magnifying glass works.

questions.q: What is the frequency of a wave?
options: The distance between two adjacent peaks
The time for one wave to pass
The number of complete waves passing a point each second
questions.explain: Frequency is the number of complete waves (or oscillations) passing a point per second, measured in hertz (Hz). The time for one wave is the period.

questions.q: A spectral line normally at one wavelength is observed at a LONGER wavelength in a galaxy's light. What does this tell us about the galaxy?
options: It is stationary relative to us
It is moving away from us (receding)
questions.explain: A shift to longer wavelength is a red-shift, which means the source is moving away from us. The bigger the shift, the faster it recedes.

questions.q: Within the visible spectrum, which colour has the highest frequency and shortest wavelength?
questions.explain: Violet light has the shortest wavelength and highest frequency of the visible colours, while red has the longest wavelength and lowest frequency.

questions.q: A green filter is placed in front of a white light source. What colour of light passes through?
questions.explain: A colour filter transmits its own colour and absorbs the rest. A green filter lets green light through and absorbs the other colours of white light.

questions.q: A blue jumper appears blue in white light because it:
options: Absorbs blue light and reflects the rest
Reflects blue light and absorbs the other colours
questions.explain: An opaque object reflects the colours we see and absorbs the others. A blue jumper reflects blue light and absorbs the remaining colours of white light.

questions.q: What is observed in the light from distant galaxies?
questions.explain: Light from distant galaxies is red-shifted — its wavelength is increased (shifted towards the red end). This shows the galaxies are moving away from us.
